paragraphs.heading: What a star is
paragraphs.text: A star is a glowing, roughly round ball of plasma held together by its own gravity. The Sun is the star nearest to Earth. Many other stars show up in the night sky, but they are so far away that they look like fixed points of light. The observable universe holds an estimated 10²² to 10²⁴ stars, yet only about 4,000 can be seen with the naked eye, and all of those lie in the Milky Way.

paragraphs.heading: How a star lives
paragraphs.text: A star begins when a cloud of gas, mostly hydrogen and helium with traces of heavier elements, collapses under gravity. For most of its active life it shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. That fusion gives off energy, which travels out through the star and radiates into space. A star's total mass mainly decides how it changes over time and how it ends.

paragraphs.heading: How a star ends
paragraphs.text: When fusion stops at the end of a star's life, what is left of its core is a stellar remnant, which can be a white dwarf, a neutron star or, for a massive enough star, a black hole. Stars and their remnants make almost all the natural chemical elements heavier than lithium, a process called stellar nucleosynthesis. Stars lose mass, or blow it out in supernova explosions, returning chemically enriched material to the interstellar medium. Those elements are then recycled into new stars.

paragraphs.heading: Reading starlight
paragraphs.text: Astronomers work out a star's mass, age, chemical makeup, variability, distance and motion by observing how bright it looks, studying its spectrum and tracking how its position in the sky shifts over time. Stars can form systems with other objects: some have planets, and some orbit one or more other stars. When two stars orbit close together, their gravity can greatly change how each one evolves. Stars also often belong to much larger groups held together by gravity, such as star clusters and galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Stars in human history
paragraphs.text: Stars have mattered to civilizations all over the world. People have used them in religion, divination and mythology, to navigate, to mark the seasons and to set calendars. Early astronomers told apart 'fixed stars', which keep their places on the celestial sphere, and 'wandering stars', the planets, which shift against them over days or weeks. They grouped bright stars into constellations to follow the planets and the Sun, and the Sun's motion against the stars gave calendars that could guide farming.

paragraphs.heading: The first star catalogues
paragraphs.text: The oldest accurately dated star chart comes from ancient Egypt in 1534 BC. Babylonian astronomers in Mesopotamia compiled the earliest known star catalogues in the late 2nd millennium BC. In Greece, Aristillus made the first catalogue around 300 BC with help from Timocharis. In the 2nd century BC Hipparchus listed 1,020 stars, a catalogue later used to build Ptolemy's. Hipparchus is also known for the first recorded nova, or new star.

paragraphs.heading: New stars and other suns
paragraphs.text: Even though the sky seemed unchanging, Chinese astronomers knew new stars could appear, and in 185 AD they became the first people known to see and describe a supernova, now known as SN 185. The brightest star event in recorded history, the SN 1006 supernova, was described by the Egyptian astronomer Ali ibn Ridwan and by several Chinese astronomers. In Europe, Tycho Brahe spotted new stars, which hinted that the heavens could change. In 1584 Giordano Bruno suggested that stars were like the Sun and might have planets of their own, an idea raised earlier by Democritus and Epicurus.
